Test this through a paper exercise: given an entirely fictional equipment fault description (model, operating hours, symptoms, accompanying sounds or alerts, recent usage and maintenance) and service conditions, write the user interview and troubleshooting sequence, checks and measurements needed, possible fault causes and verification methods, disassembly, assembly, and replacement points, and situations requiring equipment use to stop and the issue to be reported.

Signals worth considering further: willingness to troubleshoot systematically rather than replace parts based on experience alone, acceptance of seasonal peaks and on-site work, willingness to keep learning new models and electronic control systems, and ability to document the rationale in service records. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to read technical materials and circuit diagrams, compromising warranty or safety requirements, or treating customer equipment as an opportunity for arbitrary trial and error.

First assess whether you are willing to diagnose and service equipment systematically in workshops and fields over the long term, accept seasonal and on-site work arrangements, and keep learning new models and electronic control systems; test this through this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

Farm Equipment Mechanics and Service Technicians' daily work centers on a fault diagnosis and servicing cycle: ask users about symptoms and equipment usage, review maintenance and repair request records, and locate faults through observation, listening, and instrument measurements; disassemble and assemble equipment, replace damaged parts, and service hydraulic, drivetrain, braking, and electrical systems; make adjustments and conduct test runs after assembly, and document repairs and parts used; also maintain tools and testing equipment and perform warranty and recall work according to manufacturer requirements.

Work context | Farm Equipment Mechanics and Service Technicians work across repair workshops and field sites, completing a service cycle through fault interviews, testing and measurement, disassembly, assembly and replacement, system servicing, adjustment and test runs, documentation, and warranty work.
Work locations | Farm equipment dealer workshops, farm and ranch machinery sheds, fields, and irrigation sites; some positions involve traveling in service vehicles to users' sites.
Working conditions | Primarily physical and manual work, requiring prolonged standing, bending, and lifting parts, with exposure to oils and fluids, dust, and noise; working hours extend considerably during busy farming seasons, and nighttime or emergency site visits may be needed.

Collaboration | Work with workshop supervisors, parts storage and parts staff, equipment users and farm managers, and manufacturer technical support.

entries.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Three (medium preparation), SVP 6.0–<7.0. In the education survey, approximately 52% reported requiring a postsecondary certificate, 43% a high school diploma, and 3% an associate degree. BLS lists a high school diploma and long-term on-the-job training as typical entry preparation. Mainland China generally requires related secondary vocational, technical school, or higher vocational education and position and manufacturer training; work involving lifting, electrical systems, and similar tasks also requires specialized training under safety requirements. Specific requirements are subject to recruitment announcements and manufacturer requirements.

entries.answer: A more accurate judgment is that tools will assist some tasks and the occupation overall will primarily experience augmentation and structural adjustment. The ILO's 2023 study shows large differences in task exposure between occupations, and technical feasibility does not mean employer adoption. Fault determination, disassembly and assembly operations, and safety confirmation require physical measurements and on-site experience, so the conclusion is that working methods will change rather than the occupation being replaced entirely.

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of workers' wage distribution within the same statistical period, not starting pay. Overtime, on-site service, and strongly seasonal work arrangements are common in this occupation; individual income also depends on equipment type, region, and compensation definitions.
